entities.summary:
Chen Zhuo (born c. 235 CE), a pivotal figure in Chinese astronomy during the Three Kingdoms period, synthesized and significantly advanced the cartography of the celestial sphere. Active within the court of the Kingdom of Wu, his work transcended mere observation, establishing a standardized framework for star cataloging and astronomical measurement that would profoundly influence East Asian cosmology for centuries. Operating in an era marked by intense political fragmentation and intellectual ferment, Chen Zhuo's contributions provided a bedrock of empirical data and theoretical organization for understanding the cosmos, thereby cementing his legacy as a foundational astronomer and cosmographer.

Chen Zhuo's monumental achievement was the compilation of the 'Star Catalogue of Chen Zhuo' (Chen Zhuo xing jing), completed around 270 CE. This comprehensive work integrated the observational traditions of three prominent earlier schools: those of Gan De, Shi Shen, and Wu Xian. By meticulously cross-referencing and reconciling their disparate records, Chen Zhuo cataloged a remarkable 1,299 stars, grouping them into 283 constellations. He also precisely mapped the positions of the 28 lunar mansions (xiu), which served as crucial reference points for tracking planetary motion and determining seasonal changes. His methodology established a rigorous standard for celestial mapping, providing a practical guide for navigation, calendar reform, and astrological prognostication within the imperial administration.
